title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Scammers deployed voice cloning and deepfake technology to impersonate immigration attorneys, financial advisors, and family members in order to defraud residents of Georgia and South Florida. The impersonation happened on social media platforms and through phone calls using spoofed numbers. These systems were built and used entirely outside their intended purposes, with no authentication layer between the victim and the fraudster.

The failures occurred at the point of contact with the victim. No mechanism verified the identity of the person on the phone or behind the social media account before the victim sent money or shared sensitive information. The scammers obtained audio samples of their targets from public sources, then fed them to voice-cloning tools that exist for legitimate purposes. The victims had no way to distinguish a deepfaked call or video from a genuine one without additional verification steps like calling back through a known phone number.

It is not established whether the voice-cloning and deepfake tools themselves contained safety measures that were bypassed, or whether they lacked such measures entirely.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence and deepfake technology to commit fraud across Georgia and South Florida. The FBI reported that Americans lost nearly $893 million to AI-enabled scams in 2025, with criminals using voice cloning, fake photos, and spoofed phone numbers to impersonate trusted individuals. In one case, a South Florida immigration attorney discovered criminals had cloned his voice to target immigrants, while a Cobb County couple lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints totaling $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia documented 71 complaints amounting to over $10.4 million.

Authorities identified common AI-assisted scams including the grandparent scam, romance schemes, and emergency distress calls where criminals use audio samples to create convincing fake communications. Financial institutions warn that these impersonation attempts are becoming harder to detect. The Georgia Attorney General recommends establishing a family code word to verify identity, verifying urgent requests through known phone numbers, and avoiding immediate action on unexpected contact. Experts predict these scams will continue evolving as AI tools become more affordable and accessible.
